extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, civic educators, and general readers interested in public opinion and democratic procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for how public opinion, representative procedure, intelligence work, and civic education should be organized and used in democratic governance; includes when and how to appeal to the public or to reason. Emphasizes expert mediation, procedural safeguards, media-literacy education, and the limits of reason in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared ideas of federal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Federalism swings either towards imperial centralization or towards parochial anarchy wherever the union is not based on correct and commonly accepted ideas of federal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas do not arise spontaneously; they must be pieced together by generalization based on analysis, and the instruments for that analysis have to be invented and tested by research. Stable federal institutions require commonly accepted conceptual foundations developed by systematic inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms must overcome subjectivism of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: No reform, however sensational, is truly radical, which does not consciously provide a way of overcoming the subjectivism of human opinion based on the limitation of individual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective reforms must provide mechanisms that shift knowledge sources from inward conscience to objective engagement with the environment (facts, reports, expert analysis). Electoral devices or manipulations do not by themselves remedy subjectivism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of intelligence bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Primarily, the intelligence bureau is an instrument of the man of action, of the representative charged with decision, of the worker at his work, and if it does not help them, it will help nobody in the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence systems are mainly aids to representative government and administration (help decision-makers do public business better). Their value as general information sources or checks on the press is secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public can judge procedure but not technical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The outsider can ask experts to tell him whether the relevant facts were duly considered; he cannot in most cases decide for himself what is relevant or what is due consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens can evaluate procedural aspects (whether interested groups were properly heard, whether a ballot was honestly taken, whether results were honestly accepted) and should focus on these when assessing public decisions rather than attempting technical judgments beyond their competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting public appeals for expert deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the practice of appealing to the public on all sorts of intricate matters means almost always a desire to escape criticism from those who know by enlisting a large majority which has had no chance to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on mass publicity or the loudest voice to win verdicts is an anti-pattern; appeals that aim to mobilize uninformed majorities to avoid expert scrutiny undermine sound decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist issues pass procedural filters before public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Only by insisting that problems shall not come up to him until they have passed through a procedure, can the busy citizen of a modern state hope to deal with them in a form that is intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues should be filtered through representative bodies, hearings, or mediators who require expert analyses and force discussion to address facts rather than slogans. This preserves intelligibility for the general public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of neutral chairmen and expert analysts in deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The partisan voices should be there, but the partisans should find themselves confronted with men, not personally involved, who control enough facts and have the dialectical skill to sort out what is real perception from what is stereotype, pattern and elaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conferences or hearings a neutral chairman should call upon intelligence experts (accountants, statisticians, etc.) to replace vague slogans with concrete data (e.g., wage tables), rule on jurisdictional disputes, and require evidence rather than unsupported partisan claims. Private, unverifiable evidence should not determine public policy without scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and jurisdictional clarity in public hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: What is private does not interest us, says the chairman, and, therefore, issues a statement to the public announcing that the wages of workers... and that Judge Gary declines to increase them for reasons that he refuses to state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When participants refuse to make reasons public or refuse to submit evidence, officials should state the facts and the refusals publicly and direct further appeals to appropriate standing intelligence committees. Clear rules about what matters are within the hearing's jurisdiction should be enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of expert mediation to disintegrate partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of expert mediation is not that it sets up opinion to coerce the partisans, but that it disintegrates partisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert mediation clarifies facts and terminology, reducing emotionally charged stereotypes and preventing uninvolved citizens from being entangled by partisan rhetoric. The aim is clarification, not coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise naming and definition to separate emotion from idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of naming, the effect, that is, of saying that the labor groups C and M, but not X, are underpaid, instead of saying that Labor is Exploited, is incisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and name specific groups and conditions rather than using broad, emotionally laden abstractions. Objectifying ideas through precise labels makes them more open to correction by data and less bound up with personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-education must be grounded in evolving social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of this education will depend upon the evolution of knowledge. And our knowledge of human institutions is still extraordinarily meager and impressionistic. The gathering of social knowledge is, on the whole, still haphazard; not, as it will have to become, the normal accompaniment of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic education should be informed by systematic intelligence work and social science data; as decision-making requires more information, research must become routine and educational content must reflect developing knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic education: media-literacy and critical habits
rubrics_metrics.description: He can, by the use of the case method, teach the pupil the habit of examining the sources of his information. He can teach him, for example, to look in his newspaper for the place where the dispatch was filed, for the name of the correspondent, the name of the press service, the authority given for the statement, the circumstances under which the statement was secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to scrutinize sources (dispatch location, correspondent, press service, authority), assess reporter reliability, understand censorship and propaganda, use comparative history and anthropology, practice introspection about imagery and stereotypes, and employ the case method and study of error as prophylaxis against prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of appeal to reason: time and stability constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only on the premise of a certain stability over a long run of time that men can hope to follow the method of reason... For the rate at which reason, as we possess it, can advance itself is slower than the rate at which action has to be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoned approaches are most practicable where decisions allow long-term planning and stability. In emergencies or rapid-change situations, intuition, force, or urgent rhetoric may be unavoidable; political thinkers must study the time-differential between discovery and action when proposing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish false crises from real ones and plan for long durations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a factor here which realistic and experienced men do take into account... how the relevancy of any plan depends upon the length of time the operation requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing policy or appeals to reason, calculate whether assumed data will remain valid over the operation's timeframe; favor measures where longer-term reasoning can reasonably be applied and avoid imposing long plans on rapidly shifting conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards for appeals to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only insist that [hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying] have no place in the appeal to reason, that in the longer run they are a poison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public discourse and appeals to reason should reject hatred, intolerance, secrecy, fear, and lying. Cultivate decency and good will as practical moral premisses even when reason cannot prove their efficacy in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wit and force to build footholds for reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We can make a belief in reason one of those intuitions. We can use our wit and our force to make footholds for reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When immediate full rational persuasion is impossible, employ rhetoric, policy maneuvers, or institutional changes strategically to create conditions in which reasoned deliberation can later take hold; nurture long-range beliefs in reason through practice and education.
